t:
In exercising his authority to acquire property by exchange, the Secretary may accept title to any non-Federal property within the boundaries of the park and recreation areas and in exchange therefor he may convey to the grantor of such property any federally owned property under his jurisdiction in the State of Washington which he classifies as suitable for exchange or other disposal.

The values of the properties so exchanged either shall be approximately equal, or if they are not approximately equal the values shall be equalized by the payment of cash to the grantor or to the Secretary as the circumstances require.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that an exchange with a non-federal grantor brings an outside party into a federal decision. But this only authorizes a property transaction and the equalization of values; it sets up no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue. The Secretary alone classifies the federal land as suitable for exchange, so no outside party takes part in the decision.
fable.s: the Secretary may accept title to any non-Federal property within the boundaries of the park and recreation areas and in exchange therefor he may convey to the grantor of such property any federally owned property under his jurisdiction

qwen_block.w: This section authorizes the Secretary to engage in property exchanges with non-Federal owners. It describes a transactional mechanism (buying/selling/swapping land) rather than a process for outside parties to participate in federal decision-making, such as through consultation, advisory boards, or public comment. The non-Federal party is a counterparty in a transaction, not a participant in the governance or policy formulation process.
qwen_block.s: In exercising his authority to acquire property by exchange, the Secretary may accept title to any non-Federal property within the boundaries of the park and recreation areas and in exchange therefor he may convey to the grantor of such property any federally owned property under his jurisdiction in the State of Washington which he classifies as suitable for exchange or other disposal.

opus.w: This section only authorizes the Secretary to exchange land and to balance values with a cash payment. The non-federal grantor is a party to a property deal, not someone consulted before a federal policy decision. Deals like this fall under the contract exclusion. The Secretary alone decides which property is 'suitable for exchange,' and the section requires no consultation, hearing, rulemaking or right to sue.
opus.s: the Secretary may accept title to any non-Federal property within the boundaries of the park and recreation areas and in exchange therefor he may convey to the grantor of such property any federally owned property under his jurisdiction in the State of Washington which he classifies as suitable for exchange or other disposal.
opus.b: The tempting reading is that this is participation because a non-federal grantor trades property with the Secretary. That fails the definition. A land exchange is a two-party deal, much like a contract, and the definition excludes contracts. Nothing here requires the Secretary to consult outsiders, hold a hearing or comment period, issue regulations, or give anyone a right to sue before deciding.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the Secretary to acquire property through exchange with non-federal parties. While it involves interaction with outside parties (grantors), it is a transactional mechanism for land acquisition, not a process of consultation or coordination with outsiders to inform a federal decision. The definition excludes applications and transactions where the outside party is merely a counterparty rather than an advisor or participant in the decision-making process. There is no requirement for public comment, advisory boards with outside members, or consultation with states/tribes on policy.
qwen_chat.s: In exercising his authority to acquire property by exchange, the Secretary may accept title to any non-Federal property within the boundaries of the park and recreation areas and in exchange therefor he may convey to the grantor of such property any federally owned property under his jurisdiction in the State of Washington which he classifies as suitable for exchange or other disposal.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Secretary exchanges property with a "grantor" (a private party or non-federal entity), this constitutes participation. However, the definition explicitly states that "applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses" are not participation, and more broadly, simple transactions or acquisitions where the outside party is merely a counterparty to a deal (selling land) rather than a consultant or advisor in a decision-making process do not qualify. The section describes a mechanism for property acquisition/exchange, not a process of consulting with outsiders to inform a policy or regulatory decision. The "grantor" is a seller, not a participant in the governmental decision-making process in the sense defined (e.g., advisory board, public comment, consultation on policy).
